S9.title: Charlie Haden – The Liberation Music Orchestra (Impulse, 1969) and The Ballad Of The Fallen (ECM, 1982) ***** — The Free Jazz Collective review (Stef Gijssels, 5 March 2007)

continuity_case: This record extends the canon's 1960s lineage forward by the most literal route an ECM album can take: the Liberation Music Orchestra was founded in 1969 out of the Ornette Coleman diaspora — Haden from the classic Ornette quartet, Cherry and Redman from Ornette's bands, Motian from the Bill Evans Trio and the Paul Bley groups — and this is that ensemble tradition, arranged by Carla Bley out of the Jazz Composers' Orchestra world, reconvened thirteen years later with six younger players. The repertoire is itself inherited: Spanish Civil War songs from the same songbook the 1969 debut drew on, extended forward to the 1970s revolutionary song movements of Portugal (José Afonso), Chile (Ortega/Quilapayún) and El Salvador. The improvisational language is the 1960s free/post-bop large-ensemble language, disciplined by Bley's writing into march, waltz and chamber-horn textures. The case does not depend on the label: the predecessor was on Impulse!, and this record with this personnel would argue identically on Impulse! or JCOA — the ECM production documents the band, it does not constitute it.
overlap_risk: free-jazz — the LMO sits on the free-jazz/avant-garde seam: the 1969 predecessor is free-jazz-gate material, and both Wikipedia and AllMusic classify this record Avant-garde Jazz / Experimental Big Band rather than post-bop or modal. Secondary seam: experimental large-ensemble/big-band territory. The dispatch-level dedup check for this candidate already returned clean, and no modal-jazz prior claim applies — this is not a Jarrett-type late-modal record.
scope_flag: ECM gate, 1980s stretch — recorded November 1982, released 1 October 1983: inside the 1969-1985 window but among the post-1979 arrivals that lean scope_call/contested doubly. The boundary to name: this is not a late-modal or standards-continuity record; its continuity runs through the 1960s free-jazz orchestral and political tradition, and its source classification (Avant-Garde Jazz, Experimental Big Band) sits further from the canon's quartet-based post-bop core than any ECM record yet proposed. Strongest case against: a twelve-piece horn ensemble playing Spanish Civil War and Nueva Canción repertoire is arguably a different kind of artifact from the small-group lineage the canon is built on, and part of its standing rests on the ECM house production and the label's own curation of its reception. Strongest case for: DownBeat's 1984 critics poll named it jazz album of the year on the American side, independently of the label (S2), and the personnel are as load-bearing as any 1980s record's — the canon's Ornette lineage reaches directly here through Haden, Cherry, Redman and Motian.

ballot.album: Charlie Haden — The Ballad of the Fallen (1983)

scope_check.boundary_note: Recorded in November 1982 and released in 1983, it is within the 1945–1985 window, but triggers the doubly sensitive 1980–1985 tail, the 1980s ECM continuity test, and the opened free-jazz/avant-garde gate. Its continuity runs through the 1960s free-jazz and large-ensemble lineage rather than the canon's preferred modal-continuity path.

ballot.case_for: This is a load-bearing reunion of the Ornette and post-1960s avant-garde diaspora: Haden, Don Cherry, Dewey Redman, and Paul Motian are joined by Carla Bley and a twelve-piece ensemble whose lineage reaches into the Jazz Composers' Orchestra world (S1, S2, S3). The Liberation Music Orchestra's 1969-to-1983 descent, with inherited Spanish Civil War and Latin American revolutionary repertoire reshaped into disciplined march, waltz, and chamber-brass textures, makes the album a genuine mature statement rather than a merely good ECM release. Its independent contemporary reception was substantial: DownBeat named it 1984 Jazz Album of the Year and also awarded Haden and Bley top category honors (S2), while Penguin Guide gave it 3.5 stars and Rolling Stone's Jazz Record Guide gave it 4/5 (S2).
ballot.case_against: The bridge to this canon is real but indirect: the album is classified as avant-garde jazz and experimental big band, and its continuity is with free-jazz orchestral politics rather than the modal/post-bop tradition that anchors the ECM gate (S1, S2). Consensus evidence is thinner than the strongest canon standard—no major published canon-list placement is documented, Penguin's 3.5-star rating is respectable rather than core-level, and the substantive merit case relies heavily on one contemporary critics' poll and one specialist review (S2, S9). The twelve-piece political suite may be a distinct large-ensemble artifact rather than an essential entry point for the canon's center of gravity, especially if the stronger 1969 Liberation Music Orchestra statement is the project's primary representative.
ballot.disagreement: Reference 1 makes the stacked boundary decisive and calls for scope_call/consider, while Reference 2's presented case gives greater weight to the album's landmark reception, mature defining statement, and discovery value; the supplied excerpts therefore preserve a real tension between treating this as a boundary decision and treating it as a strong quality case.
ballot.recommendation: John should treat this as a serious but non-automatic audition for the canon, with the 1969 Liberation Music Orchestra album and the album's free-jazz/ECM boundary considered before deciding.
